1.note: Micah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How sorrowful I feel]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the gatherings of summer fruit** and **the gleanings of the grape harvest** are what remains after everything worth having has already been taken, so is the land in which Micah is searching for a faithful person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like one searching where the summer fruit has already been gathered, like one searching where the grapes have already been harvested]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gatherings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trying to gather summer fruit after others have already picked all of it]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gleanings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like what is left over after others have harvested the grapes]
Here, **my soul** represents Micah himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I desire]

2.note: Micah says **All of them lie in wait for bloodshed** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Nearly everyone lies in wait for bloodshed]

Micah is not referring to a specific **faithful one**. He means faithful people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [All the faithful people have perished]

Micah is not referring to a specific **upright one**. He means upright people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there are no upright people among mankind]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people who live in the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of the people that are left in the land]

Here, **bloodshed** represents violent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are just waiting to murder each other]

Here Micah is speaking the people of the land exploiting each other as if they were trappers that are trying to catch an animal **with a net**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man seeks to trap his brother]

Micah is speaking as if a man’s **brother**, or fellow Israelite, were his prey, whom he hunts to harm rather than someone he should love and protect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man tries to harm his fellow Israelite]

3.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [doing evil things]

Here, **the two hands** represent the leaders who use them to do evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [these leaders]

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the judge is also asking for the recompense]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recompense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be paid]

Micah is not referring to a specific **great one**. He means people in positions of power in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and important people are speaking the desire of their very souls]

Here, **his very soul** represents the great one himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of what he himself strongly desires]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he himself desires]
The pronoun **they** refers to all of the powerful leaders. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and these leaders weave it together]

Here Micah is speaking of the plot that these leaders are scheming together as if it were a net that they **weave** together. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they plot it out together]

4.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a brier** wounds anyone who touches it, so is even the best person among these people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [injures anyone who comes near, just as a brier does]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a thorn hedge** injures those who come near it, so is the one who seems to be one of **the upright** people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the upright person injures people even more than a thorn hedge injures those who come near it]

Micah is using the adjective **the upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the most honest person]

Micah is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time and **your watchers** represents the prophets, who warned the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The time that your prophets warned you about]

The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Israel, whom Micah addresses directly here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your watchers, people of Israel, your visitation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **visitation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when God comes to punish you]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confusion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When that happens, they will be confused and panic]

5.note: Micah is using **guard the doors of your mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be very careful about what you say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you should guard what you say]

6.note: Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a daughter-in-law is rising up against her mother-in-law]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe **enemies** who are characterized by their relationship to **a man**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The ones who oppose a man]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe **the men** who are characterized by living in **his house**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way as modeled in the UST.

7.note: Micah is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will watch** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between himself and the people he has been describing. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But unlike these people, I will watch for Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who saves me]

Moses is not using this possessive form **My God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather Moses is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom I worship,]

8.q: אַֽל־תִּשְׂמְחִ֤י אֹיַ֨בְתִּ⁠י֙ לִ֔⁠י כִּ֥י נָפַ֖לְתִּי קָ֑מְתִּי כִּֽי־אֵשֵׁ֣ב בַּ⁠חֹ֔שֶׁךְ יְהוָ֖ה א֥וֹר לִֽ⁠י
8.note: In verses 8 through 10 Micah speaks on behalf of his people. If it would be helpful, you could translate the singular pronouns as plurals, as in the UST.
By **my enemy**, Micah refers to the nation that Micah foresees will conquer Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you enemy nation of my people]

Here Micah is speaking on behalf of the people about suffering defeat as if it were to have **fallen** down and of recovering as if it were to **arise** again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we have suffered disaster; we will be restored]

Here Micah is speaking of the trouble his people are experiencing as if it were **the darkness** and of Yahweh’s help as if it were **a light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are in trouble; Yahweh helps us]

9.q: זַ֤עַף יְהוָה֙ אֶשָּׂ֔א כִּ֥י חָטָ֖אתִי ל֑⁠וֹ
9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I have sinned against Yahweh, I will bear his rage]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rage**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how Yahweh rages against me]

Micah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [pleads my plea]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just for me]

Here Micah is speaking as if Yahweh’s rescue of him were bringing him out into **the light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will rescue me]

Here Micah is speaking as if experiencing what Yahweh does were to **look on** it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will experience his righteous acts]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on how righteous he is]

10.note: The pronoun **my** refers to Micah, who speaks here on behalf of his people, and **my enemy** and **her** refer to the nation that Micah foresees will conquer Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then may the enemy nation of my people see, so that shame covers them]

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the end of the last verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Then may my enemy also see what Yahweh has done]

Micah is saying what he wants his enemy to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that my enemy see] or [Please allow my enemy to see]

Here Micah is speaking as if **shame** were a garment that **covers** a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that she becomes utterly ashamed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that she feels ashamed]

The enemy is using the question form to mock Micah by suggesting that Yahweh is unwilling or unable to help him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God is nowhere to be found!]

The enemy is not using this possessive form **your God** to indicate that Micah possesses or controls Yahweh but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God that he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom you worship]

Micah is using one part of a person, his **eyes**, to mean all of him in the act of watching his enemy’s downfall. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will watch what happens to her]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the mud of the streets** is trampled underfoot and despised, so will Micah’s enemy be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as thoroughly despised as the mud that people tread on in the streets]

11.note: Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [A day will come to build your walls]
The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Zion. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your walls, people of Zion]

12.note: The pronoun **you** refers to Zion, or Jerusalem, and the pronoun **he** refers to each person who will come to the city of Jerusalem from the distant places named in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when many people will come to Jerusalem]

13.note: Micah uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast between the restoration that he has just described and the desolation that will come upon the rest of the earth. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But all the rest of the land will become a desolation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate]

The pronoun **her** refers to the land, and the pronoun **their** refers to the people who live in the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the land’s inhabitants, from the fruit of those people’s deeds]

Here Micah is speaking of the results of what people do as if they were **the fruit** that a plant produces. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the results of their deeds]

14.note: Here Micah is speaking as if Yahweh were a shepherd and as if Yahweh’s people were **the flock** that he tends. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Care for your people as a shepherd cares for his flock, the people who belong to you]

The word translated as **Shepherd** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request to a superior rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request to a superior. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please shepherd your people]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe **the flock** that is characterized by being **your inheritance**, that is, the people whom Yahweh has chosen to belong to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the flock that belongs to you]

Micah is saying what he wants Yahweh to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that they graze] or [Please allow them to graze]

15.note: The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh did wonderful things in **the days of your going out from the land of Egypt**, so he will do wonderful things for his people again. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as I did wonderful things when you came out from the land of Egypt]

The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, who begins to speak here, and the pronoun **him** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, will make my people Israel see]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [marvelous things that I do]

16.note: Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The nations will see what Yahweh has done]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the mighty things they thought they had done]

Micah is using **put a hand over mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be too astonished to speak.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will be too astonished to speak]

Here, **their ears** represents their ability to hear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they will lose their ability to hear]

17.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the serpent** crawls low along the ground in the dust, so will the nations be brought low before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They will be brought low, licking the dust like the serpent that crawls along the ground]

The pronoun **They**, here and throughout this verse, refers to the nations mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The nations will lick]

The point of this comparison is that just as **crawling things of the earth** creep along the ground, so will the nations come out of their strongholds in fear and humiliation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like creatures that creep along the ground in fear]

Micah is using this possessive form **our God** to mean that Yahweh is the God whom he and his people worship, not that they possess or control him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly as modeled in the UST.

The pronoun **you** could refer to: (1) Yahweh, since his judgment makes sinners afraid, and the next verse addresses Yahweh directly, or (2) Israel, since Israel is addressed directly in verse 15, with no indication that that has changed. Alternate translation: [because of you, Israel]

18.q: מִי־אֵ֣ל כָּמ֗וֹ⁠ךָ נֹשֵׂ֤א עָוֺן֙ וְ⁠עֹבֵ֣ר עַל־פֶּ֔שַׁע לִ⁠שְׁאֵרִ֖ית נַחֲלָת֑⁠וֹ
18.note: Micah is using the question form to declare that no other god is like Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No other God is like you, Yahweh, bearing iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance!]

The expressions **bearing iniquity** and **passing over transgression** mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [fully forgiving all the sinful actions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bad things people do]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what people have done wrong]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe **the remnant** that is characterized by being **his inheritance**, that is, the people who belong to Yahweh who have remained faithful to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for those people who belong to him because they are still faithful to him]

Even though Micah is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person using **his** and “he”. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these pronouns throughout this section in the second person for consistency as modeled in the UST.

Here, **his nose** represents Yahweh’s anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He does not hold on to his anger forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being faithful to his covenant]

19.note: Here Micah is speaking as if the sins of his people were enemies that Yahweh will **subdue**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will overcome the power of our iniquities]

The pronouns **our** and **their** both refer to Micah and his people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all of our people’s iniquities, and you will throw into the depths of the sea all of our sins]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things we have done]

Here Micah is speaking as if the sins of his people were objects that Yahweh could **throw into the depths of the sea**, where no one could ever recover them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will completely remove all of their sins forever]

The pronoun **you** refers to Yahweh, whom Micah addresses directly here after speaking about him in the previous sentence. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and you, Yahweh, will throw]

20.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trustworthiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [proof that you are trustworthy]

Here, **Jacob** and **Abraham** represent the descendants of these two men. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to Jacob’s descendants, covenant faithfulness to those who descended from Abraham]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you will faithfully keep the covenant promise you made to Abraham]
Here, **fathers** represents “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.
